slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 6: Managing Ownership with Smart Pointers. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

slides.title: 6.1 Expressing Exclusive Ownership with std::unique_ptr
keyPoints: std::unique_ptr<T> represents exclusive ownership of a dynamically managed object through its deleter.
It cannot be copied, because copying would create another exclusive owner.
It can normally be moved when responsibility should pass to another owner.
Prefer exclusive ownership when one object or scope is clearly responsible for lifetime.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 6, treat 6.1 Expressing Exclusive Ownership with std::unique_ptr as a design decision with costs and evidence. std::unique_ptr<T> represents exclusive ownership of a dynamically managed object through its deleter. It cannot be copied, because copying would create another exclusive owner. It can normally be moved when responsibility should pass to another owner. Prefer exclusive ownership when one object or scope is clearly responsible for lifetime. Borrowing access does not require changing that ownership policy. slides.title: 6.1.2 Transferring Unique Ownership
keyPoints: Moving a unique pointer transfers its ownership and leaves the source empty under the library’s specified move.
The receiving object now controls destruction.
Passing a unique pointer by value to a function therefore makes ownership transfer visible at the call boundary.
Moving a unique pointer transfers its ownership and leaves the source empty under the library’s specified move.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 6, treat 6.1.2 Transferring Unique Ownership as a design decision with costs and evidence. Moving a unique pointer transfers its ownership and leaves the source empty under the library’s specified move behavior. The receiving object now controls destruction. Passing a unique pointer by value to a function therefore makes ownership transfer visible at the call boundary. A function that only reads the object should usually accept the object by const reference or a documented pointer, not demand ownership transfer. A function that optionally observes it can accept a nullable borrowed pointer. Choose the interface based on the relationship needed by the callee, not merely the representation used by the caller. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: 6.2.1 Understanding Reference Counting
keyPoints: Shared pointers coordinate ownership through a control structure associated with the shared lifetime.
Copying a shared pointer adds an owning participant; destroying or resetting one removes that participation.
std::make_shared creates an object with a compatible shared ownership arrangement.
The stored pointer and the managed ownership identity are not always identical concepts, as aliasing constructors.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 6, treat 6.2.1 Understanding Reference Counting as a design decision with costs and evidence. Shared pointers coordinate ownership through a control structure associated with the shared lifetime. Copying a shared pointer adds an owning participant; destroying or resetting one removes that participation. std::make_shared creates an object with a compatible shared ownership arrangement. The stored pointer and the managed ownership identity are not always identical concepts, as aliasing constructors demonstrate, but ordinary application code should begin with straightforward ownership. Never create unrelated shared ownership groups independently from the same raw pointer. Each group can then try to destroy the same object, defeating the intended coordination. slides.title: 6.2.2 Recognizing Shared-Ownership Costs
keyPoints: Reference counting adds bookkeeping, and shared lifetime can make destruction happen at an unexpected point when.
The pointee is not automatically thread-safe merely because shared ownership bookkeeping supports certain.
Reference counting adds bookkeeping, and shared lifetime can make destruction happen at an unexpected point when.
Avoid using use_count() as a synchronization or exclusive-access proof.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 6, treat 6.2.2 Recognizing Shared-Ownership Costs as a design decision with costs and evidence. Reference counting adds bookkeeping, and shared lifetime can make destruction happen at an unexpected point when the last owner disappears. The pointee is not automatically thread-safe merely because shared ownership bookkeeping supports certain concurrent operations on separate shared-pointer objects. Avoid using use_count() as a synchronization or exclusive-access proof. Another owner can appear, and the count does not describe raw borrowers. Performance and concurrency requirements need their own design. A shared pointer is a lifetime mechanism, not a mutex, a transaction, or a guarantee that access patterns are race-free. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 6, treat 6.3.1 Recognizing Cyclic References as a design decision with costs and evidence. An owning cycle can keep every strong count positive even after external roots are removed. In a parent/child model, choose which direction owns. The example gives the parent strong ownership of children while each child holds only a weak reference to its parent. Not every graph should be forced into this pattern. A central arena or registry can own all nodes while edges use non-owning identifiers, often making lifetime simpler. The important step is to draw the graph and distinguish ownership edges from navigation edges. A data relationship does not automatically need an owning edge. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 6, treat Trace the hierarchy’s ownership edges as a design decision with costs and evidence. The root has one child in its vector, and the child has a weak parent link. The local child variable is another strong owner of the child. Resetting the root therefore destroys the root and releases its ownership of the child, but the child remains alive through the local variable. Its parent observation expires. Resetting the last local child owner then ends the child’s lifetime. These intermediate states are intentional. A test expecting both nodes to disappear immediately after root.reset() would misunderstand the remaining local owner. Draw every strong edge, including test variables, before interpreting reference-counted lifetime. Hidden owners in lambdas, containers, and fixtures are common reasons for apparently mysterious retention. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 6, treat Failure clinic — The observer that owned the answer as a design decision with costs and evidence. A test creates a second shared pointer called observer, resets the original owner, and expects destruction. The object remains alive because the observer is not an observer at all; it is another owner. Renaming the variable cannot change the policy. Replace it with a weak pointer when the test only needs to detect lifetime, or accept that a strong owner deliberately extends lifetime. Another defect uses shared_ptr(existing.get()). The pointer value looks right, but the new ownership group is unrelated to the existing one. A sanitizer may later report double deletion, yet the repair belongs at construction: copy the existing shared pointer or redesign the transfer. Do not run the double-owner defect in the normal suite; reason about the invalid ownership and keep the shipped examples defined. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 6, treat Guided lab — Publish an immutable snapshot as a design decision with costs and evidence. Use the ownership-snapshot laboratory in Appendix B. Publish an owned snapshot through shared_ptr<const Snapshot>, obtain two reader owners, and retain a weak observer. Replace the publisher’s current pointer with a new snapshot. The old readers should still observe the original values until they release their owners; the publisher should expose only the new values. Verify that releasing one reader does not expire the old weak observer while the other reader remains. Then release the final reader and verify expiration. Attempt a weak promotion after expiration and require an empty result. This models lifetime across revisions without threads or a hidden global cache. The pointee is not automatically thread-safe merely because shared ownership bookkeeping supports certain concurrent operations on separate shared-pointer objects.

chapter.title: Shared lifetime and weak observation
chapter.caption: Either shared owner keeps the managed object alive. A weak observer does not; lock obtains temporary shared ownership only while the object still exists. unique_ptr uses a separate exclusive-ownership model, illustrated by the linked transfer example.
